passage:
Teacher's note, Nursery B, Tuesday. Rehana
At painting time I told Jyoti, "Put on your apron now." She folded her arms and said, "No! I don't want." Then she pushed the apron off the table. I didn't repeat the order. After a minute I held up two aprons and asked, "The blue one with stars, or the yellow one?" Jyoti pointed at the yellow one, pulled it over her head by herself and asked me to tie the back. She painted happily for twenty minutes.
Next: I'll offer two choices at tidy-up time too 🙂

qa.q: What did Jyoti do with the apron when first told to put it on?
qa.a: She pushed the apron off the table.

qa.q: Why do you think Jyoti said no to the apron at first?
qa.a: Being told "now" made it feel like an order, and saying no let her feel in charge of herself.

qa.q: What choice did Rehana make that turned things around?
qa.a: Instead of repeating the order, Rehana offered two aprons, so Jyoti could pick one and put it on happily by herself.

qa.q: How might the other children at the painting table be affected by how Rehana handled it?
qa.a: Painting time stayed calm instead of becoming a struggle, so they could keep painting without waiting or watching a scene.

grounding: A preschooler refuses an apron when ordered but puts one on happily when offered a choice of two.

passage:
Morning on the farm outside Wardha. His mother, Urmila, had the lunch tiffin ready for the cotton field. "Darshan, wear your chappals. The stubble will cut your feet." Darshan, five, sat on the doorstep and tucked his feet under him. "No. I'm not wearing."
"Darshan, now."
He shook his head hard.
Urmila put the tiffin down. She fetched his green rubber boots too and set both pairs in front of him. "Chappals or boots? You pick."
Darshan looked at them for a long moment, then jumped into the boots. "I'm wearing BOOTS," he told the hens, and marched off ahead of her.

qa.q: What did Urmila have ready for the cotton field?
qa.a: The lunch tiffin.

qa.q: Why did Darshan tuck his feet under him when told to wear chappals?
qa.a: Being ordered made him want to refuse; hiding his feet was his way of keeping control over what he did.

qa.q: What did Urmila do differently the second time, and why did it work?
qa.a: She set out both chappals and boots and let him pick, so either choice was safe and Darshan felt he was the one deciding.

qa.q: What was it like for Urmila when Darshan refused?
qa.a: She was probably in a hurry with the tiffin ready and worried about the stubble cutting his feet, so the refusal likely tested her patience.

grounding: A five-year-old refuses chappals because he is ordered to, then happily chooses boots when given two safe options.

passage: I'm Aadhya, Anshul's sister, and I've watched this all summer. In June, Papa saw Anshul chatting with the older boys who race scooters behind the stadium. That night Papa said, "You will not go near those boys. Final." Anshul didn't argue. He just said, "Fine." Before that, I honestly think he found them a bit boring. But the next week he was there every evening, and by July he was riding pillion on the fastest scooter, no helmet. When Papa took away his cycle, he walked there. My friend Ira, who lives near the stadium, says he's the loudest one in the group now. I can't see inside his head. But every new rule seems to push him one step closer to them.

qa.q: What did Papa say about the older boys in June?
qa.a: "You will not go near those boys. Final."

qa.q: Why might Anshul have started going to the stadium every evening after Papa's order?
qa.a: He had found the boys a bit boring, so the firm ban, not the boys, seems to have made them tempting; going there let him feel his choices were still his own.

qa.q: Which different choice by Papa might turn things around?
qa.a: Instead of more bans, Papa could calmly explain what scares him about riding without a helmet and agree on some limits with Anshul, leaving less to push against.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel watching all this?
qa.a: She seems worried and helpless, seeing her brother take bigger risks as each new rule pushes him further away 😟

grounding: A sister watches her teenage brother do exactly what he was firmly forbidden, with the pressure making a risky group more tempting.

passage:
Monday: Mahima found the gaming café receipt in Deepak's school bag. "You will never set foot in that place again. Do you hear me?" Deepak, fifteen, said nothing and went to his room. He hadn't even planned to go back; the games there were old.
Wednesday: He told his mother he had extra maths class and went to the café straight from school. He stayed till eight, not really enjoying it, glancing at the door every few minutes. When two older boys invited him to ride along to the highway at night, he almost said yes.
Saturday: Mahima sat on the edge of his bed. "I was scared, so I shouted. Here's what actually worries me: the late nights and those older boys. Can we work something out together?" Deepak stared at the floor for a long time. Then he said, "Friday afternoons at Sameer's house instead?"

qa.q: Where did Deepak say he was going on Wednesday?
qa.a: He told his mother he had extra maths class.

qa.q: Why did Deepak go to the café on Wednesday even though he wasn't enjoying it?
qa.a: The shouted ban made going feel like protecting his freedom, so the café mattered more as a way to push back than as fun.

qa.q: What was the turning point on Saturday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Mahima admitted she shouted out of fear, explained her real worries and asked to work it out together, which gave Deepak a say instead of an order.

qa.q: What was Monday like for Mahima?
qa.a: She was frightened by the receipt and reacted with anger, probably hoping a firm rule would keep her son safe.

grounding: A teenage boy does the opposite of a harsh ban and is drawn toward risk, until the pressure is replaced with reasons and choice.

passage:
In their Lajpat Nagar flat, Harish had a rule for every hour of fifteen-year-old Parul's day: home by six, no friends' houses, phone on the dining table after nine. By March he noticed things. Her messages were always deleted. She said she'd been at the library when a neighbour had seen her at the park. Once she slammed her door and didn't speak to him for two days.
One night Harish sat on the step outside her room. "I've been making rules without telling you why. Here's why: the main road is dark after seven, and I get scared. Can we choose together? Park with friends till seven, and you text me when you leave."
Parul opened the door a crack. "And the phone?"
"Your call, after ten."
The next evening she texted him from the park gate at five to seven: "Coming home. Want samosas?"

qa.q: What did a neighbour see that didn't match Parul's story?
qa.a: A neighbour had seen her at the park when she said she'd been at the library.

qa.q: How did Harish feel about Parul's secrecy, and what shows it?
qa.a: Harish felt scared for Parul and wanted to reconnect, which is why he sat on the step outside her room and admitted the dark main road frightens him.

qa.q: Which change in Harish's approach turned things around, and why?
qa.a: He explained the real reason for his worry and offered choices within limits, so Parul had room to decide and no need to hide.

qa.q: How might Parul have experienced her father's rules before that night?
qa.a: They probably felt like a cage with no reasons, so hiding and lying seemed the only way to have any life of her own.

grounding: A father sees his strict rules breed secrecy and defiance, then explains his reasons, offers choices within limits and reconnects.

passage:
"Kishore, sit. I'm not going to shout."
"That's new."
"Fair." Ujjwal pulled a chair close. "Last month I banned your late cricket evenings on the ground. Since then you've lied twice about where you were. Your mother found your kit in Faisal's car."
"Because you never listen, Papa. You just say no."
"You're right. I said no without reasons. Here's the reason: the ground has no lights and the road back is a highway. I lie awake."
Kishore looked up.
"So, choices. Weekend games, any time till dark. Or weekday games if someone's parent drives both ways. You pick."
"...Weekends. And Faisal's dad can drive sometimes."
"Deal. And tell me the score after. I actually want to know."
"You hate cricket."
"I like you."

qa.q: Where did Kishore's mother find the cricket kit?
qa.a: In Faisal's car.

qa.q: Why did Kishore answer "That's new" when Ujjwal said he wouldn't shout?
qa.a: Kishore expected another telling-off and felt guarded and a bit bitter, because past talks had only brought bans.

qa.q: Which choice did Ujjwal offer, and why did it work better than the ban?
qa.a: He let Kishore pick between weekend games till dark or weekday games with a parent driving, which kept the safety limit while giving Kishore a real say.

qa.q: How had the ban felt from Kishore's side?
qa.a: To Kishore it felt like being refused without being heard, so lying seemed easier than talking.

grounding: A father notices his ban led to lies, and shifts to giving reasons, offering choices within limits and showing interest.

passage:
Vaibhav: society made a new rule. every guest must be registered at the gate app 😠
Vaibhav: like I'm in school. I'm 24
Yamini: haha. so are you going to refuse?
Vaibhav: was about to write an angry post in the group
Vaibhav: wait
Vaibhav: let me think. am I angry at the rule or just at being told
Yamini: 🤔 good question
Vaibhav: honestly... there were two thefts in B wing last month
Vaibhav: registering my friends takes like ten seconds
Vaibhav: it's the tone of the notice that annoyed me. ALL CAPS
Yamini: so?
Vaibhav: so I'll register my guests and suggest they write the next notice nicer 🙂
Yamini: very grown up of you, bhai

qa.q: What does the society's new rule say?
qa.a: Every guest must be registered at the gate app.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling before he typed "wait"?
qa.a: He was irritated and ready to write an angry post, because the rule made him feel treated like a schoolboy at twenty-four.

qa.q: Which question helped Vaibhav choose his response, and what did he decide?
qa.a: He asked whether he was angry at the rule or at being told; seeing that the rule made sense, he chose to register guests and suggest a kinder tone for notices.

qa.q: What would change for the society committee if Vaibhav had sent the angry post?
qa.a: The committee might have faced a fight in the group and grown defensive, instead of getting a calm suggestion it could actually use.

grounding: A young man feels irritated by a rule, asks whether he objects to the idea or just to being told, and chooses his response deliberately.

passage: When Thomas took over the family pepper garden in Wayanad, Noor, the young agriculture officer, came by with a clipboard. "You're spraying too often. Follow the schedule in this leaflet and keep a record, or the cooperative won't buy your pepper this season." Thomas felt his jaw tighten. His father had farmed this land for thirty years without a leaflet. He almost said, "Who asked you?" Instead he walked to the tap and washed his hands slowly. Is it the advice I hate, he asked himself, or being told, by someone younger, on my own land? He read the leaflet that night. The spraying part made sense; the record book was only paperwork. Next morning he phoned Noor. "I'll follow the spray schedule. Can you show me how to fill in the record?"

qa.q: What did Noor say would happen if Thomas didn't keep a record?
qa.a: The cooperative won't buy his pepper this season.

qa.q: Why did Thomas's jaw tighten when Noor gave the advice?
qa.a: Being told what to do on his own land, by someone younger, felt like a challenge to his father's thirty years of farming and to his own freedom 😠

qa.q: What did Thomas do in the moment that helped him respond well?
qa.a: He walked to the tap and washed his hands slowly, giving himself time to ask whether he disliked the advice or just being told.

qa.q: How might Noor feel when Thomas phoned the next morning?
qa.a: Noor would likely be relieved and pleased, perhaps having expected resistance from a new farmer, and glad to help with the record.

grounding: A young farmer bristles at advice, checks whether he objects to the idea or to being told, and deliberately chooses to follow the useful part.

passage:
Tuesday: The class group buzzed at four: "Half-yearly results on the school app!" Yash, fourteen, put his phone in the drawer and went to play football till dark. At dinner his mother, Rashmi, asked, "Results?" "Not out yet," he said, and his stomach turned.
Friday: At maths tuition, Sir began going over the half-yearly paper. Everyone else had checked their marks and brought questions. Yash hadn't looked. He sat with his notebook closed, heart thumping, not following a word.
Sunday: Rashmi found him awake at one in the morning. He finally opened the app with her beside him. Maths was bad: 41. Science was fine. "Okay," Rashmi said. "Now we know what to fix." Yash let out a long breath. The number was smaller than the fear had been.

qa.q: Where did Yash put his phone when the results came out?
qa.a: He put his phone in the drawer.

qa.q: Why might not checking the app have felt better to Yash on Tuesday?
qa.a: Avoiding the marks postponed the sting of a bad result, so for a few hours he could pretend nothing had changed.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Opening the app on Sunday with his mother beside him; once he knew maths was the problem he could start fixing it, and the fear shrank 🙂

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt finding Yash awake at one?
qa.a: She probably felt worried and tender, realising the results had been weighing on him for days.

grounding: A teenage boy avoids checking his results to put off the sting, and the not-knowing leaves him more anxious and lost in class.

passage: Sahil, you've been hiding that report card envelope under your pillow since Friday. Your Mola Dolma knows everything. Let me tell you about my brother Pasang. In Darjeeling, when we were young, results were pinned on the school gate. Pasang was fifteen. The day they went up, he took the long road home, round the tea garden, so he wouldn't pass the gate. For two weeks he wouldn't let anyone say the word "results". He barely slept, and he snapped at our mother. Then the teacher came to our house. Pasang had failed one subject, and the re-test was in four days. Four days, when he could have had two weeks. He passed, just. But he always said the waiting was worse than the marks. So. Shall we open it together, over tea?

qa.q: Why did Pasang take the long road home round the tea garden?
qa.a: So he wouldn't pass the gate where the results were pinned.

qa.q: Why do you think Pasang wouldn't let anyone say the word "results"?
qa.a: Hearing it brought the dread closer, so blocking it out gave him a little relief, even though he barely slept.

qa.q: What choice does Dolma offer Sahil, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To open the envelope together over tea, so Sahil faces the news early and with company, leaving time to act instead of losing days to fear.

qa.q: What might those two weeks have been like for Pasang's mother?
qa.a: She had to live with his snapping and sleepless nights without knowing why, which was likely worrying and hurtful.

grounding: An elder recalls a brother avoiding his results, which left him anxious and with less time to prepare for a re-test.

passage:
Tushar: why did your card get declined at the canteen
Omkar: idk. bank server probably
Tushar: have you checked your balance?
Omkar: not since october 😬
Omkar: the last message said something about a fee and I just... stopped opening them

passage: The government college in Hosur put attendance on the notice board outside the office every Monday. In August, Deepak's name was in yellow: 71 percent. He'd been missing early lectures to help at his uncle's tyre shop. After that, Deepak took the side stairs on Mondays, the ones that avoided the board. It felt better not knowing. When Mahima asked, "Did you see the list?", Deepak said, "Yeah, yeah, it's fine." By October the office sent a letter home: attendance too low to sit the semester exams without the principal's approval. His mother read it out in the kitchen, her voice shaking. Deepak remembered August, when a few weeks of mornings would have fixed it.

qa.q: What colour was Deepak's name on the board in August?
qa.a: Deepak's name was in yellow.

qa.q: Why did taking the side stairs feel better to Deepak?
qa.a: Not seeing the board spared him the worry each Monday, so avoiding it gave quick relief even while the problem was growing.

qa.q: When could Deepak have fixed things most easily, and how?
qa.a: In August, when his name first turned yellow; talking to his uncle about the shop hours and going back to early lectures would have fixed it.

qa.q: What might the letter have been like for Deepak's mother?
qa.a: She was clearly shaken, likely frightened for his studies and hurt that she hadn't known sooner 😢

grounding: A student stops looking at attendance records once they turn bad, and a small problem grows into a serious one.

passage:
March, a Tuesday: Usha, a freelance illustrator, found a reminder letter under the door: she had missed a filing deadline, and there was a late fee. She hadn't opened her accounts in months. She sat on the floor feeling sick.
April, first Sunday: She asked her calm flatmate Imran to sit with her for one hour, with tea. Laptop open: money in, money out, clients who hadn't paid, the health check she'd half booked, work deadlines. She wrote each in a notebook. It was ugly but short.
May, first Sunday: Same hour, same tea. This time the notebook showed one client two weeks late and her dentist reminder due. She sent one polite email and booked the appointment. Twenty minutes, and she shut the laptop smiling.

qa.q: What did Usha find under the door in March?
qa.a: A reminder letter: she had missed a filing deadline, and there was a late fee.

qa.q: What does Usha shutting the laptop smiling in May suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt calm and in control, because the problems were small and caught early instead of piling up.

qa.q: Which choice in April turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Setting a fixed hour with Imran and a notebook to look at money, health and work together; with calm company the bad news was bearable, and it got smaller each month.

qa.q: How might Imran experience sitting with Usha that first Sunday?
qa.a: Imran may have felt trusted and useful, simply by staying calm while Usha faced something hard.

grounding: A young woman moves from avoiding her accounts to a monthly hour with a calm friend, so bad news arrives small and early.

passage: Lokesh, you keep saying the accounts scare you, so sit and listen to an old man. I'm Shankar, and when I was twenty-five, I ran the night shift at this very press, and I was a champion at not looking. Unpaid bills went in a drawer. The doctor's reminder card went in the same drawer. Then one year the drawer exploded: a supplier stopped our paper, and my knee, which I'd ignored, needed months of rest. My friend Govind, a quiet schoolteacher, said, "Every Friday at five, I'll come with two cups of tea. We open the drawer together." So we did. Ten minutes some weeks, an hour others. Bad news still came, but it came small: one late payment, one appointment to book. Forty years later I still do my Friday. Tomorrow's Friday, Lokesh. I'll bring the tea.

qa.q: Where did young Shankar put the unpaid bills?
qa.a: Unpaid bills went in a drawer.

qa.q: Why might hiding bills in a drawer have felt reasonable to young Shankar?
qa.a: Not looking spared him the worry for a while, so the drawer gave quick relief even as the problems grew inside it.

qa.q: What choice turned things around for Shankar, and why did it work?
qa.a: Opening the drawer every Friday at five with Govind and tea; a fixed time and calm company meant bad news arrived small and early.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel when Shankar says he'll bring the tea tomorrow?
qa.a: Lokesh might feel relieved and less alone, knowing someone calm will be there while the accounts finally get opened.

grounding: An older man recalls learning to face money, health and work papers at a fixed weekly time with a calm friend, and offers the same to a younger colleague.

passage:
"Pranav, you've skipped dinner again."
"Not hungry, Ishita. Stomach's a bit off."
"It's been 'a bit off' since Diwali. I've seen you pressing your side on the stairs."
"It's nothing. Probably gas. If I go to a doctor, they'll find something, then tests, then..."
"So you'd rather not know?"
Pranav went quiet. "Something like that."
Ishita sat down beside her brother. "I'm not going to nag. I'll book the clinic for Saturday morning and come with you. You do the talking, I'll hold the file. If it's gas, we get chaat after."
"And if it's not?"
"Then we'll know early, and the doctor will tell us what's next. Either way, you're not going alone."
Pranav let out a breath. "Saturday. But you're buying the chaat."

qa.q: What has Ishita seen Pranav doing on the stairs?
qa.a: Pressing his side on the stairs.

qa.q: What is Pranav afraid of when he avoids the doctor?
qa.a: He fears a visit will uncover something serious and lead to tests, so not knowing feels safer for now.

qa.q: Which choice by Ishita helped Pranav agree, and why?
qa.a: Instead of nagging, Ishita booked the clinic and offered to come along and hold the file, so he didn't have to face it alone.

qa.q: How might Ishita's offer feel from Pranav's side?
qa.a: It likely felt like relief rather than pressure: someone handling the practical steps and staying beside him, so the fear felt smaller.

grounding: A sibling notices her brother avoiding a check-up out of fear and offers gentle company to the doctor instead of pressure.

passage: Last winter my older sister Kiran coughed through the nights in the room we share in Ludhiana. She'd laugh it off: "Winter throat." I tried pressure first. I forwarded her scary articles, and once I told her in front of Mummy that she was being stupid. She just coughed more quietly, into her pillow, and stopped mentioning it. That frightened me more than the cough. So one evening I changed tack. "I'm going to the clinic on Thursday for my own check-up. Come with me? Kulfi after." She was quiet, then nodded. In the waiting room she held my hand like when we were kids. The doctor listened properly and gave her a plan to follow. What helped wasn't my arguing. It was sitting beside her. I'm Baljeet, and I'm still learning that.

qa.q: What did Kiran call her cough?
qa.a: Winter throat.

qa.q: Why did Kiran start coughing more quietly into her pillow?
qa.a: The pressure made her feel judged and scared, so she hid the cough rather than face it or be argued with.

qa.q: What turning point does Baljeet describe, and why did it work?
qa.a: Inviting Kiran along to a shared clinic visit with kulfi after; gentle company felt safe, while arguing had only pushed her to hide it.

qa.q: What was that waiting room like for Kiran?
qa.a: She was probably frightened, holding Baljeet's hand like a child, but comforted not to face the doctor alone 🤍

grounding: A sibling learns that pressure made a sister hide her symptoms, while gentle company to the clinic and a doctor's advice helped.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was Dashami, and my uncle Tapan gave me three hundred rupees for Puja! I went straight to the sweet shop with Chaitanya and bought rasgullas, sandesh, a big bag of jhalmuri and a toy gun that pops. All three hundred gone by six o'clock. Best day.
Then Chaitanya said, "Why don't you spend your piggy bank money on sweets too?" I said NO WAY. That's my saved money, ten rupees every Sunday from Baba since summer. Didi says I'm the richest boy in the house because of it. I would never waste it on sweets.
Chaitanya said, "But money is money." I said it's not the same. Puja money is for fun.
Now I'm in bed with a stomach ache and thinking. Is it the same? It doesn't feel the same.
Pradeep

qa.q: What did Pradeep buy with the Puja money?
qa.a: Rasgullas, sandesh, a big bag of jhalmuri and a toy gun that pops.

qa.q: Why does the piggy bank money feel different to Pradeep from the Puja money?
qa.a: He saved it slowly, ten rupees every Sunday, so it feels precious, while the gift money came all at once and felt meant for fun.

qa.q: What could Pradeep try the next time he gets festival money?
qa.a: He could drop part of it into the piggy bank first and spend the rest, treating it like the money he works to save.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya see the two kinds of money as the same?
qa.a: Chaitanya isn't attached to Pradeep's saving story, so three hundred rupees is simply three hundred rupees, whichever pot it sits in.

grounding: A boy spends all his festival gift money on sweets but would never spend his saved pocket money that way.

passage:
At the Pongal fair in their village near Thanjavur, Gopal had a hundred rupees from Thatha tied in his handkerchief. Before sunset it was gone: two rounds on the giant wheel, a paper windmill, and four packets of candy floss, one after another. On the way home his sister Minakshi said, "You still have forty rupees in your tin at home, from selling mangoes with Appa. Want to buy the flute you liked tomorrow?"
Gopal shook his head hard. "That's my mango money. I worked for it."
"It's the same rupees," Minakshi said.
"No it isn't," said Gopal, holding his sticky fingers away from his shirt.
Their mother, Sharmila, laughed quietly. "Same rupees, different feelings," she said.

qa.q: How much money did Thatha give Gopal?
qa.a: A hundred rupees, tied in his handkerchief.

qa.q: Why won't Gopal spend the mango money on the flute?
qa.a: He earned it selling mangoes with Appa, so it feels hard-won and precious, unlike Thatha's gift, which felt free to spend.

qa.q: What could Gopal try at the next fair?
qa.a: He could decide beforehand to keep some of the gift money in his tin, giving it the same care as money he earned.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see her brother's spending at the fair?
qa.a: Minakshi seems puzzled and a bit amused that Gopal spent a hundred rupees on candy floss but won't touch forty for a flute he really wanted.

grounding: A boy spends festival gift money freely at a fair but refuses to spend the smaller amount he earned himself.

passage: I'm Suraj, Wasim's neighbour in the chawl. Wasim gets up at five every day to deliver newspapers, and he keeps that money in a steel box under his bed. He won't even buy a vada pav from it. "That's for my phone," he says. Last Sunday he won player of the match at the inter-colony cricket final: a thousand rupees in an envelope. By evening he had treated eight of us to falooda, bought new batting gloves and a cap he didn't need, and topped up his game credits. When I asked why he didn't put it in the steel box, he looked at me like I was mad. "Prize money is for enjoying, yaar." I don't know exactly what goes on in his head. But a rupee is a rupee, isn't it?

qa.q: Where does Wasim keep his newspaper money?
qa.a: In a steel box under his bed.

qa.q: Why does Wasim feel prize money is for enjoying while newspaper money isn't?
qa.a: The newspaper money comes from waking at five every day, so it feels earned and serious, while the prize arrived all at once and felt like a bonus for fun.

qa.q: What could Wasim do the next time he wins prize money?
qa.a: He could put part of it in the steel box before celebrating, so the prize also helps the phone he works so hard for.

qa.q: How might Suraj and the other friends see Wasim's falooda treat?
qa.a: They probably enjoyed it and saw Wasim as big-hearted, though Suraj also wonders why a prize rupee feels different to Wasim from an earned one 🤔

grounding: A neighbour watches a teenage boy guard his earned money but spend a prize in a day, as if the rupees were different.

passage:
Eid, Monday: Ayesha Khala pressed two thousand rupees into Irshad's hand. "Eidi, for you." By Wednesday he had spent most of it: a gaming headset, burgers for his cricket team and a pair of sunglasses. It felt light and easy, like money from nowhere.
The next Saturday: Irshad did his usual shift at his uncle's grocery, stacking rice bags, and was paid three hundred. His classmate Kavitha asked to borrow fifty for a notebook. "No way," he said. "I sweated for that."
Two weeks later: The school trip form came: eight hundred rupees. Irshad counted what was left: the three hundred in wages and forty rupees of Eidi. He stared at the sunglasses on his desk. "It was all the same money," he said out loud to the empty room.

qa.q: What did Irshad buy with the Eidi?
qa.a: A gaming headset, burgers for his cricket team and a pair of sunglasses.

qa.q: How did Irshad feel about his wages compared with the Eidi?
qa.a: Irshad felt protective of the wages he had sweated for and refused to lend any, while the Eidi felt light and easy, so he spent it in days.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Irshad, and what could he do differently next time?
qa.a: Counting his money for the trip form showed him that all rupees are the same; next time he could set aside part of any gift before spending.

qa.q: How might Kavitha have felt when Irshad refused fifty rupees?
qa.a: Kavitha may have felt hurt or surprised, having seen Irshad spend freely on burgers and sunglasses only days before.

grounding: A teenage boy spends gift money quickly while guarding his wages, until a trip form shows him every rupee counts the same.
